timeline: You could buy a dead man's sins for sixpence in old Wales, but who eats the bread?
Everyone pictures outcasts swallowing sins for sixpence.
But the real history is stranger.
Historical accounts describe poor men hired at funerals to take on the dead's sins.
A loaf of bread was handed across the coffin.
The sin-eater drank a bowl of ale.
For sixpence, he took all the deceased sins.
Villagers shunned them as unclean outcasts.
Yet some wealthy farmers secretly revived the custom.
Did poor villagers really eat bread off a corpse?
